expectations.text: At least two separate ILAC blocks (Law and Application parts)
Every Issue is framed as a question ("Whether ..." or ends with ?)

expectations.text: Application is longer than Law in every ILAC block
Discussion has a comparison table with an ICCPR column
Reference list with at least 6 entries
Status of laws flagged (in force / amended / repealed)
Ratio decidendi and obiter dicta both identified
Application reasons element by element against the facts
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Each ILAC block walks through the court's reasoning step by step with paragraph cites (e.g. ILAC 1: Act is 'existing law' (paras 7, 17-18), then Nordin Salleh distinguished on two grounds (para 15), then Art. 10(2) read with Art. 162 (paras 23-25)); ILAC 3 ties the holding back to Azmi's actual remarks.

expectations.text: Application gives the strongest argument for both sides on contested points
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] ILAC 1: 'On one hand, this is orthodox... On the other hand, the defence's textual point has force'; ILAC 3 sets the prosecution's mapping of tendencies onto Art. 10(2)(a)/(4) against critics who say the three limbs were never worked through, plus ICJ and Article 19.

expectations.text: Application compares the facts with decided cases (analogises or distinguishes a precedent)
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Distinguishes Nordin Salleh (State law, post-Merdeka), departs from Sivarasa and Mohd Nasir Hashim in favour of Pung Chen Choon, and notes Mat Shuhaimi (2016) later tested s. 3(3).

expectations.text: Every Conclusion answers its Issue directly and states a degree of certainty
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] 'Yes... This holding is firm and binds lower courts'; 'No. Courts will not review... reasonable'; 'No... The holding is secure as precedent, but the proportionality analysis is thin'. Conclusion 2 is slightly weaker on certainty (the application text calls it 'the least stable part').

expectations.text: Discussion states where the chosen theory fits AND where it fits poorly
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Authoritarian theory 'fits the Act's design... fits poorly with a constitution that entrenches Art. 10 and a court that applies proportionality'; Hallin and Mancini 'fits poorly'; Habermas used as second lens.

expectations.text: Discussion explains why each comparator jurisdiction was chosen and links back to the ILAC findings
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] 'Singapore is chosen for shared colonial heritage and a recent repeal. The UK is the origin... India... a constitutional text that expressly says reasonable', which Malaysia's court declined to read in (ILAC 2). Also notes Singapore's repeal is not simply a liberal turn.

expectations.text: Uncertain or unverified points are flagged rather than stated as fact
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] '[to verify]' on the Sedition (Amendment) Act 2015 commencement, Singapore successor laws, Kedar Nath Singh, and the Mat Shuhaimi citation; notes the Columbia third quotation conflicts with the judgment and follows the judgment.

expectations.text: Ratio decidendi stated as a legal rule (not merely the order/outcome) and obiter identified as obiter
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Separate 'Ratio' paragraph states two rules ((1) Art. 162 saves pre-Merdeka laws; (2) no reasonableness review but must fall within a listed ground and be proportionate), separate from 'Outcome and order'; labels the Ooi Ah Phua criticism and drafting history 'Obiter (not needed for the result)'. The obiter label is arguable, since this reasoning supports the ratio.
